### Fixed — one unfamiliar server entry no longer hides the whole file

A remote entry labelled with any transport other than `"http"` — `"sse"`,
`"streamable-http"`, both common in Cursor, Claude Code and VS Code configs —
failed schema validation for the entire file. `scan` printed a validation
dump, exited 2, and scanned nothing in that file: a hardcoded token in the
server next to it went unreported. Remote entries now accept any `type`
label, and an entry that is neither a launch command nor a URL is skipped
with a one-line warning naming it, while every other server in the file is
still scanned. A file whose `mcpServers` is not an object is still an error.

`--live` still dials remote servers over Streamable HTTP only; a server that
speaks just the legacy HTTP+SSE transport is reported as a failed
connection, not scanned live.

`docs/rules/README.md` stopped at MCPG-502 while the registries grew to 32
rules. The table is now generated from the registries (`npm run docs:rules`),
with a "Needs" column saying what each rule requires beyond the config file
(`--live`, `--registry`, a lock file, auto-discovery), and a test fails when
it falls behind the code or a rule has no page.

Running the rule over every server in the official MCP registry showed that
most of its findings there were not values at all: 27 of 33 were `{…}` slots
(the registry's own variable syntax) and one was a key file path. The rule
now skips whole-value slots (`{name}`, `<NAME>`, `[text]`), key and
certificate paths (`./certs/server.key`, `~/.ssh/id_ed25519`), and treats any
braced reference as a reference — including VS Code and Cursor's
`${env:NAME}` and `${input:api-key}`, which were previously read as literal
values. On the same registry snapshot the rule goes from 33 findings to 5.

If you pinned a paginated server with `pin --live` before this release, the
lock holds only its first page: the next scan reports MCPG-502 for it.
Review the full tool list, then re-pin.

- **Start-up no longer loads the MCP SDK.** The SDK — and the protocol schema
  set it builds on import — is now loaded on the first live connection
  instead of on every invocation. `guardmcp --version` went from a median of
  291–307 ms to 167–173 ms on the machine measured; static `scan`, `proxy`,
  `baseline` and `init` benefit the same way.
- **Config files are parsed once.** The value was re-tokenised from the text
  after the syntax tree had already been built; it is now read off the tree.
  Line offsets are computed only when a finding needs a position.
- **Secret matching rejects ordinary values in one pass.** One combined
  prefix test runs before the per-provider patterns, instead of allocating
  five global regexes for every env value and argument.
- `npm run bench` (`scripts/bench-scan.mjs`) times `scan` over 1,000
  generated configs. Median on that run went from 720–739 ms to 502–522 ms,
  with byte-identical JSON and SARIF output. Numbers are from one 4-core
  Linux machine on Node 22 and will differ elsewhere.

`guardmcp proxy -- npx -y some-server` puts guardmcp in the config's
`command`, so MCPG-104 (shell invocation), MCPG-105 (unpinned package) and
MCPG-106 (deprecated package, with `--registry`) only ever looked at
guardmcp — wrapping a server in the proxy, as the README recommends, hid it
from them. They now check every command in the launch: the proxy itself (an
unpinned `npx -y guardmcp` is still reported) and the command it wraps,
whether guardmcp is started directly, through a package runner, or as the
built CLI under `node`, with or without the `--` separator.
MCPG-602 (listening on every interface) and the launch-argument half of
MCPG-701 read the wrapped command's arguments too, each finding reported
once at its real index; the entry's `env` is read once, for the wrapped
server the proxy passes it to.

### Added — MCPG-602: a "local" server listening on every network interface

A stdio entry started with `--host 0.0.0.0` (or `--bind ::`, `HOST=0.0.0.0`,
a Docker port published as `-p 8080:8080` with no host address) is also a
network service that anyone who can reach the machine can use, with the
credentials in its `env`. Mapped to OWASP MCP09 (Shadow MCP Servers), whose
own references measure MCP servers bound to `0.0.0.0` and reachable from
outside. Loopback binds and `127.0.0.1:` Docker mappings are not reported.

### Changed — MCPG-701 also reads launch arguments

Telemetry and logging switches given on the command line — `--log-level off`,
`--no-telemetry`, `--logging=false` — are now reported like their `env`
equivalents. `--quiet` / `-q` are deliberately not matched. The rule's title
now says "launch configuration" instead of "launch environment".

### Docs

`docs/owasp/MCP08-MCP09.md` lists, item by item, what guardmcp checks for
MCP08 and MCP09 and which parts of those categories (log pipelines, SIEM,
asset registries, network discovery) a scanner cannot see.

### Docs — the rule catalog is generated

`docs/rules/README.md` stopped at MCPG-502 while the registries grew to 32
rules. The table is now generated from the registries (`npm run docs:rules`),
with a "Needs" column saying what each rule requires beyond the config file
(`--live`, `--registry`, a lock file, auto-discovery), and a test fails when

### Fixed — MCPG-102 no longer reports placeholders and key paths as secrets

Running the rule over every server in the official MCP registry showed that

(the registry's own variable syntax) and one was a key file path. The rule

`${env:NAME}` and `${input:api-key}`, which were previously read as literal
values. On the same registry snapshot the rule goes from 33 findings to 5.
### Fixed — `--live` read only the first page of each listing

`tools/list`, `prompts/list`, `resources/list` and `resources/templates/list`
are paginated in MCP, and `--live` (and so `pin --live` and
`inventory --live`) only ever read the first page. A server could keep a
poisoned tool out of the scan by serving it on page two, while clients —
which follow the cursor — gave it to the model. Every listing is now read to
the end. A server that paginates forever (a repeated cursor, or more than 100
pages) fails its introspection with a message instead of being reported from
a partial listing.

If you pinned a paginated server with `pin --live` before this release, the
lock holds only its first page: the next scan reports MCPG-502 for it.
Review the full tool list, then re-pin.
### Performance

- **Start-up no longer loads the MCP SDK.** The SDK — and the protocol schema
  set it builds on import — is now loaded on the first live connection
  instead of on every invocation. `guardmcp --version` went from a median of
  291–307 ms to 167–173 ms on the machine measured; static `scan`, `proxy`,

  Line offsets are computed only when a finding needs a position.
- **Secret matching rejects ordinary values in one pass.** One combined
  prefix test runs before the per-provider patterns, instead of allocating
  five global regexes for every env value and argument.
- `npm run bench` (`scripts/bench-scan.mjs`) times `scan` over 1,000
  generated configs. Median on that run went from 720–739 ms to 502–522 ms,
  with byte-identical JSON and SARIF output. Numbers are from one 4-core
  Linux machine on Node 22 and will differ elsewhere.
### Fixed — a server behind `guardmcp proxy` is no longer invisible to the launch rules

`guardmcp proxy -- npx -y some-server` puts guardmcp in the config's
`command`, so MCPG-104 (shell invocation), MCPG-105 (unpinned package) and
MCPG-106 (deprecated package, with `--registry`) only ever looked at
guardmcp — wrapping a server in the proxy, as the README recommends, hid it
from them. They now check every command in the launch: the proxy itself (an
unpinned `npx -y guardmcp` is still reported) and the command it wraps,
whether guardmcp is started directly, through a package runner, or as the
built CLI under `node`, with or without the `--` separator.

### Added — `guardmcp proxy`: watch a live MCP session

```sh
guardmcp proxy [--log traffic.jsonl] [--sarif proxy.sarif] -- <command> [args...]
```

A transparent stdio proxy between an MCP client and a server — Wireshark for
MCP. Bytes are forwarded unchanged in both directions; every JSON-RPC message
is logged with its direction, kind, method, id and request-to-response latency
(to stderr, or as JSONL with `--log`). Each `tools/list` response is run
through the tool rule catalog as it passes, so a poisoned tool is flagged at
the moment the client receives it — including one that only appears
mid-session, which a one-off `scan --live` never sees. `--sarif` writes the
session's findings on exit.

The wrapped server's exit code is preserved (128 + signal number when it was
killed by one, 127 when it could not be started), SIGINT/SIGTERM/SIGHUP are
forwarded to it, and malformed input is logged as `invalid` rather than
crashing the proxy or being dropped. The `--log` file is created owner-only and
redacts credentials (credential-named keys and known-provider secrets) in the
logged copy; records are dropped and counted rather than queued without bound
when the disk falls behind. The server is spawned through `cross-spawn`, so the
`.cmd` shims Windows installs for `npx` and `uvx` work.

**Düzeltme (kritik):** `guardmcp` Linux ve macOS'ta sessizce hiçbir şey taramadan çıkıyordu.

npm bu platformlarda çalıştırılabiliri simge bağı olarak kurar (`node_modules/.bin/guardmcp -> ../guardmcp/dist/cli/index.js`). Giriş noktası kontrolü bağ yolunu gerçek dosyayla karşılaştırdığı için hiç eşleşmiyor, CLI de 0 koduyla çıkıyordu: hiçbir şey taramamış ama "temiz geçti" gibi görünen bir sonuç. 0.1'den bu yana o platformlardaki her `npx guardmcp` ve global kurulum etkilenmişti; Windows etkilenmedi (npm orada `.cmd` sarmalayıcı yazıyor).

Bağ artık karşılaştırmadan önce `realpathSync` ile çözülüyor ve derlenmiş CLI'ı bir simge bağı üzerinden çalıştıran bir entegrasyon testi eklendi; hata geri dönemez. Sorun, guardmcp'yi Linux konteyner içinde MCP kayıt defterine karşı çalıştırırken bulundu.

```
npx guardmcp@0.16.1 scan ~/.claude.json
```

### Added — MCPG-106: a server launched from a package its own registry has given up on

Found by measuring, not by imagining a threat. Four of the original reference
MCP servers — `server-postgres`, `server-github`, `server-puppeteer`,
`server-brave-search` — were pulling about **214,000 installs a week** between
them. Every one was marked deprecated on npm, their repository had been
archived for fifteen months with *"NO SECURITY GUARANTEES ARE PROVIDED"* in its
README, and the two with the most installs hold database and source-control
credentials.

Nobody installing them was told. npm's deprecation message is the one channel
that reaches every install, and on all four it was the stock text — *"Package
no longer supported. Contact Support at npmjs.com/support"* — which sends the
user to npm's help desk and names no replacement. Reported upstream as
[modelcontextprotocol/servers#4785](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/issues/4785);
this rule is the part of the answer that does not depend on anyone else acting.

```sh
guardmcp scan --registry        # ask npm about every launched package
```

```
MCPG-106  high  "github" server launches "@modelcontextprotocol/server-github",
          which npm marks as deprecated. Every published version is deprecated —
          the package is abandoned, not just this release.
```

Three choices worth knowing about:

- **Opt-in, behind `--registry`.** Every other rule runs without touching the
  network; a scanner that phones home unasked is a scanner that is hard to
  trust. The lookup is one request per distinct package, made once at the CLI
  boundary, and the rule itself stays a pure function.
- **Absence means unknown, never fine.** Without the flag the rule says
  nothing. With it, a package the registry could not answer for — offline,
  404, rate-limited — is named on stderr as unchecked and never becomes a
  finding *or* a silent pass.
- **The finding says whether the message is npm's generic default.** If the
  registry names a successor, the finding quotes it. If it is the stock text,
  the finding says so, rather than passing "contact support" along as though
  it were advice.

MCPG-105 catches the version not being pinned. This catches the case where
pinning would not help: there is no version worth pinning to, because there
will never be another one.

Not covered: `uvx` (PyPI can yank a release but cannot mark a project
abandoned, so there is nothing to ask) and whether the repository is archived
(a second lookup against a second service; the registry's own flag is the
maintainer's explicit statement and is enough).

32 rules. 695 tests.

---

```sh
npm install -g guardmcp@0.16.0
guardmcp scan --registry
```

Fixes the `action.yml` `description`, which ran to 205 characters against the GitHub Marketplace limit of 125 and blocked the listing. Shortened to 106 without dropping what the action does.

No behaviour change — same 31 rules, same CLI, same SARIF output as [v0.15.0](https://github.com/BerkantACUN/guardmcp/releases/tag/v0.15.0).

v0.1.13: precision first

On 1,340,156 lines this scanner produced exactly two expired verdicts and both
were wrong, and on drizzle-orm's 270,525 lines it reported zero markers where
grep finds seventeen. This release is those two facts, fixed.

The false claims: a file whose header shows it was copied, vendored or
generated can no longer produce a version verdict at all, and prereleases
compare properly at last — 5.0.0-0 is below 5.0.0, which closes the nuxt
false positive as well.

The misses: removal intent in the active voice, a declaration whose NAME
confesses with its adjacent comment as the reason, floor conditions written
in prose, and addresses outside GitHub with `verifiable` separating addressed
from resolvable.

The noise: generator-owned files skipped whole, deprecation notices counted
apart from workarounds, and density computed on unique reasons.

And an oracle that needs no API, opt-in behind --probe-upstream, which
produces evidence from git alone and never says open or closed.

fix: a stated intention is a condition too (E follow-up)

Measuring the release against novu at bc2776de3 found five previously-reported
markers gone, which the brief forbids: "Later we will remove this attribute"
four times in libs/maily-core, and "we will remove this in the future" in
libs/maily-render. Those are promises to delete. The guard added with E asked
for a tag in front or a when/once/after behind, and a plain intention has
neither.

So an intention counts as a condition: we will / shall / should / must / can,
or later / eventually / soon, in front of "remove this"; or "in the future"
behind it. The two lines that stay dropped are the ones that should be —
"// Remove this line not to show stack trace" describes what the code does,
and "/** Delete this message from the platform. */" is API documentation about
a method, not a note about code. Both are now fixtures, positives and
negatives alike, so this cannot regress twice.

Also renames the JSON key to skipped_generated_files, because it counts files
and the spec's "skipped_generated: 38" is a marker delta. Both numbers are
worth having and conflating them is how a number starts lying: novu skips 999
files, all of them libs/internal-sdk, and those files held exactly the 38
markers the spec predicted.

feat: ask git when the API will not answer (G)

api.github.com answers 403 from shared and datacenter IPs, and so does the web
front end, while `git clone` answers 200. That is the situation our own
scheduled runs are in, and it is the situation a customer without a token is
in. So when a reference cannot be resolved through the API, git alone can
still produce evidence: whether any commit upstream claims the issue this
comment cites, and which release contains that commit.

What it must never do is say open or closed, and it does not. "No commit
mentions #233" is the absence of a claim, not evidence that an issue is open,
and the probe never touches expired_reasons or any other verdict. L2 evidence,
never an L3 verdict — that distinction is the only reason this is allowed to
exist, so the suite pins it as a rule: every probe result is checked for the
shape of a verdict and fails if it carries one.

Opt-in behind --probe-upstream, because a tool that advertises "runs locally"
does not start cloning other people's repositories on its own. Blob-less,
no-checkout, one clone per upstream cached for the run, five upstreams per
scan, sixty seconds per git call, and the temp directory is removed after.

Verified live, both directions, in 3.2 seconds for two upstreams:
- sindresorhus/np#802 -> fix_claimed_in, commit 9582dfff 2026-07-15,
  contained in v12.0.0 — the whole evidence chain, no API call
- pacocoursey/cmdk#233 -> no_commit_references_issue, and no pull request ref
  exists upstream either. That reproduces the spec's own finding: the
  workaround citing it is alive because upstream is dormant, not fixed.

readProbe is pure and pinned by an offline table, so the boundary is testable
without a network. A version table lands with it, pinning the prerelease
ordering from H in the same place.

feat: floor conditions written in prose, and prereleases compared properly (H)

"Vite 7.3.3+ applies this automatically" asks exactly the question "fixed in
vite 5.1" asks; only the grammar differs. Two new shapes — `<pkg> <version>+`
and `<pkg> >= <version>` — feed the same floor resolver, which is what turns
the note ISSUE-A found into a verdict instead of a sighting.

A comment can name more than one package. novu's names esbuild and vite, and
only vite is in the manifest, so claims are now pooled across the whole reason
block and the one this project actually depends on is chosen. A claim about a
package nothing here declares cannot be a floor for this project; it stays
the fallback and resolves to unresolved rather than to a guess. Without that,
the first match won by accident and the answer was esbuild.

Prereleases, carried over from the nuxt false positive of 14 Sep and settled
here once for both oracles: "5.0.0-0" is BELOW 5.0.0, not equal to it. The
old comparison split on dots and read "0-0" as NaN, which compared equal,
which made a floor of ^5.0.0-0 satisfy a fix claimed in 5.0.0. The range
reader was dropping the prerelease before the comparison even saw it, so both
ends are fixed: rangeFloor keeps it, and cmpVer orders it.

Fixture A now reaches its full target — 1 marker, version_floor_watching 1,
Vite 7.3.3 against a floor of 6.4.0 with the lockfile's 6.4.3 printed beside
it as evidence, and the esbuild issue as the address. New H_prose_floor
fixture pins both prose shapes and the prerelease case, which reads watching
where it used to read expired.

Deviation from the spec, stated rather than hidden: H says resolve against
the lockfile. The verdict still stands on the manifest floor — what the
project promises to support — with the lockfile printed beside it, which is
the 0.1.12 decision and unchanged. On the fixture both give watching, so the
acceptance number is the same either way; moving the verdict onto the lockfile
is a decision about what the product claims, not a detail to slip into a
shape change.

## Public Browser 3.0.0

In a blind benchmark on our own 30-test page — five runs each, Claude Code 2.1.281, driver Claude Opus 5, Chrome 153 — Public Browser 3.0 passed 30/30 in every run with a median of **3.02M session tokens against 4.53M for agent-browser 0.38.1** (driven through its CLI): −33% tokens, −33% cost, −24% tool calls, −32% time. agent-browser passed 29/30 in every run; the one difference is T5.2, a `navigator.webdriver` check. Method, raw run JSONs and where Public Browser loses: [README → Benchmarks](https://github.com/Silbercue/public-browser#benchmarks).

**Update the server and the Python client together.** `publicbrowser` 2.0.0 ([PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/publicbrowser/)) needs Public Browser 3.0.0 or newer; `publicbrowser` 1.0.0 does not work with 3.0.0.

**Real Chrome profiles:** on macOS, site logins do not carry over through `--profile` (current Chrome does not load the profile's cookies through the link Public Browser uses). The README no longer promises a logged-in profile.

**Install in Claude Code** — the command in earlier READMEs failed with `unknown option '-y'`:

```bash
claude mcp add --scope user public-browser -- npx -y public-browser@latest
```


## Changelog

The Python client `publicbrowser` 2.0.0 is released together with this version; `publicbrowser` 1.0.0 does not work with 3.0.0 (see Breaking).

### Breaking
- **Node.js 20 or newer.** `engines` now requires `node >=20`; Node 18 is end-of-life and was not tested in CI.
- **Update the server and the Python client together.** The Script API now needs its key (see Security), and `publicbrowser` 1.0.0 does not send one: against the new server it reports `ConnectionError: Public Browser server not reachable` although the server runs, and with `auto_start=True` it starts a second server that cannot get the port and ends with `Server did not become ready`. MCP configs that run `npx -y public-browser@latest -- --script` pick up the new server on their next start, so update `publicbrowser` at the same time.
- **A real profile runs without a debugging port.** With `--profile` Chrome is driven over `--remote-debugging-pipe`; nothing listens on a TCP port. `--attach` and the Python escape hatch `page.cdp` do not work with a real profile (`/session/create` returns `cdp_ws_url: null`, `page.cdp` raises `RuntimeError`), `session.cdpPort` of the Node library is `undefined`, and a second Public Browser on the same profile stops with an error naming the PID of the Chrome that holds it (also when the temp directory path contains spaces). Should Chrome refuse the pipe, it gets a random debugging port (never 9222) and a warning.
- **CSS selectors are strict.** A selector that matches more than one element no longer acts on the first match: `click`, `type`, `fill_form`, `press_key`, `scroll`, `drag`, `file_upload` and `observe` do nothing and return up to five candidates (ref, role, name). Invalid CSS such as Playwright's `:has-text()` names a ref or valid CSS as the way out. Flows that relied on the first match need a ref or a narrower selector.
- **Refs are kept per tab and never reused.** Ref numbers keep counting across navigation and reload instead of starting again at `e1`, so a ref from a page you left reports `stale ref` instead of hitting whatever node now has that number. `switch_tab` switches the ref table instead of discarding it — refs of an unchanged tab stay valid when you come back, a ref of another tab names its tab, and a node a re-render removed reports `stale ref` instead of typing into nothing. Stored plans with hard-coded refs need fresh refs from `view_page`.
- **`run_plan` `saveAs` stores the raw result.** Hint paragraphs appended to a result (`Tip:`, `Note:`, `Warning:`, `Notice:`) and blocks the server adds next to it (click diff, dialog, download and relaunch notices) no longer end up in the variable.
- **Python API.** `page.click()` reads `"text=Sign in"` as visible text and `"e12"` / `"ref:12"` as a ref; any other string is a CSS selector (plain text and `ref:` were sent as CSS before and did not work). `page.wait_for("text=…")` waits for page text, a ref waits for the element to be visible. `page.download()` returns the download report (JSON with filename, path, size and url, or a notice) instead of a directory. `page.evaluate()` no longer returns appended hints as part of the value. `Chrome.connect()` takes `token=`, raises `ConnectionError` when another program answers on the port and `PermissionError` when a Public Browser server rejects the key.

### Removed
- `run_plan` has no `parallel` and no `use_operator` any more. Both were in the schema but always returned an error; they are gone from schema and description.
- The Cortex no longer uploads anything. The opt-in telemetry upload and its variables `PUBLIC_BROWSER_TELEMETRY` and `PUBLIC_BROWSER_TELEMETRY_ENDPOINT` are gone; the default endpoint `https://cortex.public-browser.dev/v1/patterns` never existed. Cortex patterns stay in `~/.public-browser/cortex/`.

### Security
- The Script API answers only requests that carry its key (`Authorization: Bearer <key>`, else `401`). A server started with `--script` generates the key and writes it to `~/.public-browser/script-api-<port>.token` (mode 0600); `Chrome.connect()` reads it from there, hands a fresh key to a server it starts itself, or takes `PUBLIC_BROWSER_SCRIPT_TOKEN` / `token=`. Requests with an `Origin` header or a `Host` other than `127.0.0.1:<port>` / `localhost:<port>` get `403`, which blocks web pages and DNS rebinding. `GET /health` identifies the server (`{server: "public-browser", version}`), so a client never takes another program on the port for it.
- A real profile no longer opens a debugging port that every local program could use to take over the browser running your profile (see Breaking).

### Fixed
- A click that opens a new tab names the tab's ID and title in its answer, also in the one-line step summary of `run_plan`, so `switch_tab` can use it.
- `switch_tab` works as a `run_plan` step without `action` instead of failing with `Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'isError')`; a step whose handler returns nothing (`wait_for` without `condition`, `handle_dialog` without `action`) is reported as an error.
- A click inside a cross-origin iframe that sits in another cross-origin iframe now reaches its target: nested frames are auto-attached through their parent frame, and `view_page` no longer lists iframes of other tabs, whose refs sent clicks into those tabs while reporting success. A Script API tab no longer sees or acts in the cross-origin iframes of the MCP tab.
- `drag` scrolls the source into view before it reads coordinates — elements below the fold were dragged at off-screen coordinates and nothing happened (benchmark T3.3). HTML5 drag-and-drop (draggable lists, SortableJS, React DnD) runs through `Input.setInterceptDrags` and `Input.dispatchDragEvent`. When no reaction is detected — no drop, no DOM change around source and target, no input event — `drag` answers `Drag not confirmed: …` instead of `Dragged …` (the finding opens the line, so it survives the one-line step summary of `run_plan`), without an error: only the source's document is observed, for about 250 ms after release, so iframes, shadow DOM and later updates are not seen and the answer asks to verify with `view_page` rather than repeat the drag. Scrolling, a mere text selection and changes elsewhere on the page do not count as a reaction; Public Browser's own session overlay is ignored, other `aria-hidden` elements are not. A drag on a canvas says its result can only be checked with `capture_image`.
- `press_key` sends every character once: the extra `char` event made Chrome insert each character twice (`HHeelllloo`) and each Enter as two line breaks, in inputs, textareas and editors.
- On macOS a `Control+<letter>` that changes nothing in the focused editor answers with a hint to use Meta instead of Control; nothing is remapped silently. `Meta+A`, `Meta+Z` and `Meta+Shift+Z` carry the editing commands (`selectAll`, `undo`, `redo`) Chrome needs on macOS, where these shortcuts did nothing.
- `type` accepts contenteditable editors by ref (`generic (editable)` in `view_page`, also their text children) instead of rejecting role `generic`. Text goes to the end of the editor — before, it landed in front of the existing text — or to the caret when the caret already sits there, so a `Meta+B` before `type` still applies; `clear: true` empties the editor.
- The Cortex no longer leaves `patterns.jsonl.*.tmp` and `tree-head.json.*.tmp` files behind: a failed atomic write removes its temp file, and leftovers older than 60 seconds are deleted on first access.
- The shipped starter table of the Cortex (`community-markov.json`) survives every refresh; before, the first locally recorded pattern wiped it, although the server instructions had announced it as loaded.
- `evaluate` no longer recommends `inspect_element`, a tool this server does not register.
- Script API tabs get page lifecycle events: `navigate` waits for the page instead of always running into the 15-second settle limit (about 1.5 s instead of 15 s). A session with a call still running is no longer closed as idle, so a call longer than 30 seconds (such as a long `wait_for`) ends with its own result or timeout instead of error `-32001` and a closed tab.
- Python client: a call with a tool `timeout` waits for it plus 10 seconds on the HTTP side, so the server's timeout message arrives instead of a socket `timed out`.

### Changed
- The diff shows only what changed since the last observation (no stale `REMOVED` lines, no iframe nodes), at most 15 change lines with live regions first, then controls, the rest counted as `+N more changes`. A deferred click diff that is ready when the next call starts is attached only if that call is a page action (`click`, `type`, `fill_form`, `press_key`, `scroll`, `drag`, `view_page`, `wait_for`, `run_plan`); any other tool, including `switch_tab`, consumes it without showing it. A diff still being computed when the next call starts is dropped, whatever the tool.
- Compact `view_page`: a parent's StaticText lines are dropped only when their texts, joined in order and compared without whitespace, form exactly the name on the parent's line (no substring rule), StaticText and LabelText carry no refs, and a text field's inner editor is dropped when the field's `value` shows its text. With `filter: "all"` a multi-line container name is cut to its first line, unless the container holds `aria-hidden` or `inert` text; the TRUNCATED line is shorter. With `filter: "all"` it appears only for such a container, counts the characters past the 80-character name and names no call; with other filters it still recommends `view_page(ref, filter: "all")`.
- Each tip appears at most once per MCP session (reset when a client initializes); state notes (counts, truncation) and the STOP/REFUSED warnings of the evaluate streak stay in every response.
- No `[~N tokens | N refs]` footer in `view_page` and no `Server:` line in `virtual_desk` (both values stay in `_meta`), `navigate` and `view_page` print the Cortex line only when the most likely next tool reaches P ≥ 0.9 (whenever a hint matches the page type, `_meta.cortex` carries it in full), and unambiguous `evaluate` strings come back raw in the MCP tool; strings that read as numbers, booleans, null or JSON, empty strings, `run_plan`, the Script API and the Node library keep the JSON form.
- Tool definitions cost 4,837 tokens on the wire (2.10.6: 4,990; `npm run token-count`).
- The session overlay bar shows a small link for the person watching the browser (GitHub star, or a Jev hint): first after the fifth tool call, then every 10 minutes for 20 seconds; never in headless sessions, and never again once clicked or closed (remembered in `~/.public-browser/nudge.json`). The overlay is `aria-hidden`, so agents do not see it.
- Docs: the Claude Code install command was wrong — `claude mcp add --scope user public-browser npx -y public-browser@latest` fails with `error: unknown option '-y'`. The correct command is `claude mcp add --scope user public-browser -- npx -y public-browser@latest` (README, llms-install.md, python/README.md).
- On macOS, current Chrome does not load site cookies through the profile link Public Browser uses for `--profile`, so sites start logged out; bookmarks, history, extensions and Chrome's own Google sign-in do carry over. The README no longer promises a logged-in profile. Verified with Chrome 153.
- Benchmark harness (`test-hardest/`): CLI participants (agent-browser, Playwright CLI) in the blind runs, token counts deduplicated per model message, a real-site probe and an acceptance check script. Not part of the npm package.

**Full Changelog**: https://github.com/Silbercue/public-browser/compare/v2.10.6...v3.0.0

# Applied Inference Lab: Compliance Control Embedding Stack (v1.0.0)

An open-source machine learning framework for mapping technical software vulnerabilities (CVE descriptions) to formal cybersecurity compliance controls (NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 and CMMC).

Developed by James Pusateri (Middle Coast Software Inc.) and published under the Applied Inference Lab initiative.

## Technical White Paper

The complete 9-page academic white paper is attached to this release:
- **File**: `autormf_white_paper_202609.pdf`
- **Title**: *Domain-Specific Contrastive Representation Learning Outperforms Generative LLMs and Hybrid Retrieval in Cross-Domain Compliance Mapping*

## Key Highlights & Empirical Findings

- **Zero-Shot Baselines**: Off-the-shelf embedding models achieve less than 1.0% strict top-1 accuracy out of the box (0.30% for BGE-Large, 0.10% for GTE-Qwen2-7B).
- **Contrastive Fine-Tuning**: A compact 110M parameter encoder (BGE-Base) fine-tuned with Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss (MNRL) achieves **77.45% Strict Hit Rate @ 1**, **82.15% Strict Hit Rate @ 3**, and **87.15% Parent Control Roll-up Hit Rate @ 3**.
- **Generative LLM Reranking Degradation**: Using a 7B parameter generative model (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) downstream of dense retrieval reduced top-1 accuracy from 77.45% to 72.00% as the general-purpose model over-indexed on secondary operational cues.
- **Lexical Hybrid Search Collapse**: Fusing sparse BM25 Okapi keyword matching with dense embeddings using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) caused strict top-1 accuracy to collapse to 13.65% due to lexical rank poisoning across mismatched vocabularies.
- **Edge Deployment**: Weights convert cleanly to GGUF format (Q8_0 precision) for sub-millisecond in-process inference via llama.cpp and LLamaSharp without external cloud APIs.

## Included Artifacts

- Full contrastive fine-tuning pipelines with in-batch negatives (`scripts/train_embeddings.py`).
- Parameter-efficient LoRA adapter training for high-capacity models (`scripts/train_qwen_embeddings.py`).
- Isolated 2,000-sample golden evaluation dataset (`data/golden_validation_set.json`).
- Comparative benchmarking harnesses (`scripts/evaluate_local_model.py`, `scripts/test_reranker.py`, `scripts/test_hybrid_search.py`).
- LoRA weight merging utility for GGUF conversion (`scripts/merge_lora.py`).
- Standalone SQLite database generator (`scripts/init_db.py`).

jev: attributable User-Agent; raw sends bodies as written; GREV_DEBUG=requests

- Every request now identifies the project:
  "grev/0.2.0 (pickv; linux/amd64; +https://github.com/aurorainfra/grev)".
  Tools sent "grev-tools/<version> <tool>" and jev "grev-tools/jev" with no
  version and no link back.
- jev raw sent a re-encoded body, which sorts object keys; key order is
  part of what the model reads. It now sends the body as written and only
  splices "model" in at the front when it is missing.
- GREV_DEBUG=requests prints request and response bodies (never the key).
  GREV_DEBUG takes a comma-separated list (requests,sched,seek), documented
  in the man pages.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Size requests by tokens, not bytes; fix pickv on dense logs

pickv on a 900 kB coloured log failed with 400 max_tokens_exceeded: it cut
windows at 60 kB assuming 3.6 bytes per token, but ANSI codes, digits and
punctuation put that log at 1.4 bytes per token, so each window was about
2.5x over the 32k state+question limit.

- jev: estimate text per character class, fitted on reported usage
  (letter 0.24, digit 1.26, punctuation 0.85, space ~0, other Unicode
  0.99 tokens); within ~6% of billed usage on that log. Tokens and Fit
  support running sums and token-aware cuts.
- jev: strip ANSI escape sequences and control characters (except tab and
  newline) from every state and question the model reads; output is
  untouched. About 25% fewer tokens on coloured logs.
- jev: treat 400 max_tokens_exceeded (and 413/422 over-limit) as "too
  large": split the batch and retry; a single question that still doesn't
  fit fails with ErrTooLarge. The fake server now answers like the API.
- pickv: windows of ~16k estimated tokens; a window the API rejects is
  halved and asked again. A QUESTION without "?" is asked as a description
  ("the most interesting line"): asked whether any line answers it, the
  model said no (0.03); asked whether any line fits it, yes (0.56).
- cli.Chunks (isv --chunks, grev -l): token budget, and linear instead of
  re-estimating the growing chunk on every line.
- seek --peek heads and sampled folder names, unwrap and seg windows:
  token budgets.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

trv, sortv: tr and sort by meaning

trv edits like tr (translate, -d delete, -s squeeze) or sed s/// (-e REGEX
with -r TEXT, -o 'A|B' choices, or -d), but only at the occurrences where
the model says the instruction applies. Code finds the candidates; each is
shown to the model marked ⟦like this⟧ in its line; everything else is copied
byte for byte, and replacements only ever come from the command line.

sortv orders records along a dimension described in words: a Score seed
places every record on a five-step scale with the list as context, then
odd-even passes compare neighbours pairwise, asked both ways round to

### Added
- `fast_run(url, goal, ...)`: a browser sub-task on an owned background tab, one TypeSafe Jev request per decision,
  with typed hand-backs (`Reason`), resume on the same tab, a commit gate, evidence, a trace, and a verify-ready
  `JEV_BROWSE_RESULT` line.
- Interactive helpers: `jev_open`, `jev_adopt`, `jev_find`, `jev_click`, `jev_check`, `jev_close`.
- Values from the caller, from goal-derived candidates chosen by Jev, or from a text backend after a miss, with a
  grounding gate. Personal fields are never sent to a text backend. Sensitive fields are never typed, read, or
  sent.
- Text backends: `claude` (subscription CLI, pre-started process), `codex` (subscription CLI, unmeasured),
  `ollama`, `openai` (any OpenAI-compatible endpoint), and `none`. Local and OpenAI-compatible backends run a
  known-answer canary, cached across processes, and a configurable fallback.
- One configuration surface: environment variables (including the browser-harness `.env`) over
  `~/.config/jev-browse/config.toml` over defaults (`docs/configuration.md`).
- `python3 -m jev_browse install | uninstall | doctor | config`, and `bin/jev-browse`. The installer links the
  skill for Claude Code and Codex.
- The `jev-browse` agent skill, an agent-followable `install.md`, and a global-pointer snippet.
- A benchmark (`bench/run_bench.py`) with code-only verification and list-price cost, and a text-backend eval
  (`bench/text_eval.py`).

Ports code from [browser-use/jev-ultrafast](https://github.com/browser-use/jev-ultrafast) (MIT).

Add oh-my-pi as a connect target with an Other agents menu (#589)

`whiteboard connect omp` rejected oh-my-pi as a target even though
oh-my-pi already accepts `@dev.fast/pi-whiteboard` through its `pi`
package.json compatibility and discovers the packaged skill. Users had
to translate the Pi prompt by hand.

## CLI

- `omp` is a connect target, listed in the default and `all` output and
in the argument help, labelled oh-my-pi.
- Its prompt installs the existing Pi package with `omp install
npm:@dev.fast/pi-whiteboard`, adds the optional trace-search step
through `omp install`, and verifies after `/reload-plugins` with
`whiteboard api session_get_instructions '{}'`.
- No new package or dependency. The Pi package description now says it
connects Pi or oh-my-pi.

## Desktop connect card

- The Pi tab becomes an **Other** menu after OpenCode that lists Pi and
oh-my-pi with their marks. The trigger shows the chosen agent's mark and
name, takes the active-tab look, and remembers the choice like the tabs
do.
- Pi's mark is pi.dev's `logo-auto.svg` (MIT). oh-my-pi's is drawn after
its hero image (MIT). Both are credited in `agent-logos.tsx` next to the
existing lobe-icons note.
- The menu is a new shared `OptionMenu`; the Sessions page's Filter and
Sort controls now use it instead of their local copy, so there is one
menu implementation.

Harness detection for authoring sessions is unchanged.

## Verification

- Prompt tests, connect-card and Sessions browser tests, root lint, and
typecheck pass.
- oh-my-pi 18.3.0 in a clean Docker container: the exact install line
from the prompt succeeds, `omp plugin doctor` reports the package
healthy, and a captured model request shows the whiteboard skill
advertised to the model.

Disable detached editor windows (#579)

## Why

Opening an editor in a separate window always failed with `Error:
Whiteboard does not provide status bar parts`. The stock
`AuxiliaryEditorPart` always calls
`IStatusbarService.createAuxiliaryStatusbarPart()`, and Whiteboard's
`ReviewStatusbarService` throws there on purpose. The OS window was
already open by then, so the user got a blank or half-built window that
never set up its layout or cleanup.

We don't want to support detached editor windows right now, so this PR
removes every way to open one instead of making them work.

## What changed

- **Tab drag-out:** `EditorTabsControl.isNewWindowOperation` always
returns `false`, so dropping a tab outside the window, with or without
Alt, no longer opens a new window.
- **Commands and menus removed:** Move/Copy Editor into New Window,
Move/Copy Editor Group into New Window, New Empty Editor Window, Restore
Editors into Main Window and Open Modal Editor in New Window. Their
Command Palette, tab/tab-bar/empty-group context menu and Layout menu
entries are gone too.
- **Output panel:** removed "Open Output in New Window".
- **Startup restore:** `EditorParts.restoreState` ignores detached
windows saved by older builds instead of reopening them.

The throwing status bar stub in `reviewWorkbenchServices.ts` is left as
is, so any path we missed still fails loudly.

## Reviewer notes

- The `workbench.editor.dragToOpenWindow` setting still shows in
Settings but no longer does anything.
- The terminal and chat also have "open in new window" paths, but
neither is loaded in Whiteboard.
- Not yet checked in a built app. To check: run `app:build` and
`app:run`, then confirm that dragging a tab out of the window does
nothing and that the Command Palette has no "New Window" editor
commands.

## Testing

- `tsgo --project ./src/tsconfig.json --noEmit --skipLibCheck` passes
(`noUnusedLocals` is on, so it also catches leftover imports).
- Review unit tests (`code-oss/src/vs/review/**/*.test.ts`): 197/197
pass.

Stop VS Code settings import failing on empty or malformed settings.json (#581)

## What

`readSettings` in `reviewUserConfigImport.ts` now reads a VS Code
`settings.json` the same way VS Code does:

- An empty, blank, or comments-only file counts as having no settings.
Keybindings still import.
- If the file has syntax errors (for example a missing comma), it
imports the settings the parser could still read and logs how many
errors it found.

## Why

PostHog reported `Cannot import invalid VS Code settings from …`. The
importer threw on any parse error or non-object root, so these files
aborted the whole import, keybindings included. VS Code treats all of
them as valid.

User impact before this fix (not blocking, but the import is lost):
- **Startup:** the error is caught, so the app launches normally, but
nothing is imported. Because nothing gets written, including the file
that marks the import as done, it retries and fails on every launch.
That likely sends a PostHog event each time, so event counts may
overstate the number of affected users.
- **Manual import command:** shows an error dialog with no guidance on
how to fix it.

## Tests

Added two behaviour tests: one for empty, blank, and comment-only files,
and one for recovering settings from a file with a missing comma. All 11
tests in `reviewUserConfigImport.test.ts` pass.

Symbolicate Review Desktop error stack traces in PostHog (#586)

## Problem

Desktop error reports in PostHog are unreadable. Example: [issue
01a0d4a5](https://us.posthog.com/project/492396/error_tracking/01a0d4a5-7105-7742-a9eb-64e859485e44)
shows only "An unexpected bug occurred." and frames such as
`vs/review/review.desktop.main.js:703:21307`.

- Release bundles are minified, and no source maps reach PostHog, so
frames never resolve.
- Reports group by message digest only, so every bug with that generic
upstream message lands in one issue.

## Change

- `apps/review-desktop/scripts/upload-source-maps.mjs` runs `posthog-cli
sourcemap process` (pinned 0.18.3) on `out-vscode-min`. It then writes
`out-vscode-min/review-chunk-ids.json`, which maps each bundle path to
its chunk ID.
- `compile-darwin-payload.sh` runs it after the minified build when
`REVIEW_POSTHOG_KEY` is set (release and preview). Packaging already
drops the `.map` files.
- The Review server reads the manifest from `<app>/out` and adds
`chunk_id` to each frame. A stack whose frames all resolve no longer
sets `$exception_fingerprint`, so PostHog groups it by resolved frames.
Other stacks keep the message digest.

## Before merge

Add these, or the next release/preview compile fails:

- Secret `POSTHOG_CLI_API_KEY`: a PostHog personal API key with error
tracking write scope.
- Variable `POSTHOG_CLI_PROJECT_ID`: `492396`.

## Verification

- Ran the CLI injection on a copy of a real `out-vscode-min` (24
bundles). All 26 JS files still parse. 230 sampled positions resolve to
the same source through the injected maps as through the originals.
- Unit tests for chunk ID tagging, fingerprint fallback, and manifest
reading pass. `oxlint` and `oxfmt` are clean.
- End to end on macOS: ran `compile-darwin-payload.sh`, uploaded the 25
maps to project 492396 with this script, and packaged with
`REVIEW_DESKTOP_PRECOMPILED=1 package-macos.sh`. In the packaged app, a
keydown whose `keyCode` getter throws produced an `$exception` whose
frames PostHog resolved to `extractKeyCode` (`keyboardEvent.ts:17`),
`new StandardKeyboardEvent` (`keyboardEvent.ts:152`), and `dom.ts:1835`.
The test issue is resolved.

## Not covered

- Linux (Fedora) builds: `package-linux.sh` builds and packages in one
gulp task, so the bundles would need tagging before packaging there.
- Canvas (`assets/`) frames: the Vite build emits no source maps yet.

Release editor 0.20.0: re-point a connector by dragging its endpoint

Fixing a connector that pointed at the wrong box meant deleting it and drawing a
new one, which threw away its label, routing, motion preset, and any story step
that highlighted it. Dragging an endpoint did nothing: React Flow has no default
behaviour for reconnection, and the canvas never passed onReconnect.

The edge keeps its id. That is the whole design, not an implementation detail —
motion presets and story step targets are keyed by edge id, so a delete-then-add
with a fresh id would leave the old id orphaned, sanitizeStory would strip it, and
any step whose only target was that connector would be deleted outright. Silent
data loss from what the user experienced as dragging an arrow. motion/ops.test.ts
now asserts both directions of that: the step survives while the id is present,
and disappears when it changes.

Geometry measured from the endpoint that moved does not survive, because it
describes an anchor that no longer exists — the offset for the moved end, the
manual bend, and any precomputed diagramRoute are dropped, while the offset for
the end that stayed put is kept. reverseEdgeInSnapshot set the precedent that
endpoint-scoped data travels with its endpoint.

History is pushed on drag start, matching the geometry drags, because pushing it
in onReconnect would snapshot state that already contains the change and make
Mod+Z a no-op.

Adds canConnect as one predicate for both new connections and re-pointing, which
closes two gaps that existed before this. Locked nodes were only enforced through
the node's `connectable` flag, which says nothing about reconnection —
`reconnectable` lives on the edge — so an endpoint could have been dropped onto a
locked node. And the duplicate guard lived only in connectCommand, which the
interactive drag path never used. It is wired to isValidConnection too, so the
canvas refuses a drop instead of accepting one it would then discard.

Sequence messages stay excluded, which flowEdges already anticipated: their
handles encode row geometry capped at 12 rows, and they have their own endpoint
drag. That opt-out is now explicit rather than relying on React Flow's
edgesReconnectable default.

Release editor 0.19.0: composed reference layouts over WebMCP

An agent could place elements but not compose them. Recreating a reference
diagram meant approximating it with generic shapes, because there was no way to
nest artwork inside a card, pick a specific pictogram, or set type. This adds the
three pieces that were missing.

Icons. drawcms_search_icons queries Iconify and returns exact identifiers
alongside collection and license metadata, sending only the search string — never
the diagram. Nodes then build as type "icon" with an iconName, and the editor
downloads, sanitizes and embeds the SVG itself. Raw SVG and arbitrary asset URLs
stay rejected as authoring inputs, so the agent cannot smuggle markup through a
diagram. A failed or cancelled download leaves the document untouched, and an
edit arriving mid-download is rejected as stale rather than applied to a document
that has moved.

Real membership. parentId is React Flow parentage, not visual overlap: moving a
card moves its icon, title and caption, and child positions are relative to the
parent's top-left. Missing parents and cycles are rejected. Replacement accepts
any node order and sorts it (node-hierarchy.ts); an incremental batch still has
to add a parent before its children, because there is nothing to attach to
otherwise. updateNode gains width, height and parentId, so existing artwork can
be grouped or detached without moving on screen, as one undoable batch. Deleting
a parent cascades to descendants and their edges.

Typography. Every create and update path exposes the text and shape fields the
canvas already supported — font, alignment, line height, stroke width, opacity,
border radius, z-index — so a composition can match a reference instead of
approximating it. Explicit text sizes turn textAutoResize off, since a specified
size that then resizes itself is not a specified size.

Connectors use absolute coordinates for nested endpoints and may cross their
enclosing frames. Tidy rearranges root compositions without disturbing their
children, and scope: "connectors" leaves an intentional layout alone. A story
step targeting a parent highlights its descendants, so a beat can light a whole
card; explicit connector targets still mean exactly those connectors.

public-api.test.ts gets an explicit 30s timeout. It imports the whole barrel on
purpose, which is what catches a regressed export, so it is the slowest import in
the suite and grows with the editor — it went from ~1s standalone to over the 5s
default under full parallel load once this landed. Raising the budget is honest;
trimming what it asserts would not be.

Merge pull request #17 from drawcms/fix/onboarding-template-overwrite

Stop onboarding templates overwriting the open document

Release editor 0.18.0: stop templates overwriting the open document

The onboarding chooser could destroy a saved diagram. It opened whenever a
per-browser localStorage flag was absent — a fresh profile, a second machine,
cleared storage — with no regard for what was on the canvas, and picking any
template called applyDocument() unconditionally, bypassing the guardReplace()
that File > New and import already used. On a host that persists by document id
and autosaves (cloud), that replacement was saved straight over the user's
diagram, name included, and autoplay kept it dirty so it saved repeatedly.

Extract the two decisions into onboarding/policy.ts so they are testable and
stated in one place:

- shouldAutoOpenOnboarding() requires an empty document. The dismissal flag
  cannot tell "has never seen the guide" from "is opening a saved diagram on a
  new machine"; emptiness can.
- resolveTemplateTarget() never returns a silent replace. Empty canvas loads in
  place, a host that can create documents gets the template as a new one, and
  otherwise we confirm first.

Add onCreateFromTemplate so hosts bound to a document id open a template as a
new document instead of replacing the open one. guardReplace() gains a label for
accurate confirmation copy and confirmWhenNotEmpty, which the template path opts
into: a whole-document swap has no undo and the chooser is reachable from the
File menu at any time.

Also derive the "Start from a template" summary from the catalog. It was frozen
at the original four names while the catalog grew to 18, so the guide advertised
a fraction of what the grid below it offered.

Repairs two tests left stale by b201ca4, which moved the palette's hide control
into the panel header and replaced the diagram-type select with a popover
picker. No test had ever rendered the onboarding overlay, which is how this
shipped.

commits.message:
The admission gate: a distilled team decision waits for a human

Distillation now proposes team decisions instead of publishing them. A new
team-lane decision note enters admitted = 0, invisible to recall, and shows in
the review inbox as a proposal. `motif memory admit` (confirm) promotes it into
recall and supersedes the decision it updates; `reject` (retire) keeps it in the
record but never serves it. Files, topics, personal notes and conflicts (already
adjudicated) are admitted on sight.

The gate is a live-pipeline policy, not an applyNotes default: runMemoryTick
passes gate:true, while seeds, backfills and the demo, which represent memory
the team already accepted, do not, so they land admitted. Recall, the confidence
support count and the overview decision count all filter admitted = 1, so a
proposal never counts as team knowledge until a person lets it in.

Migration v14 adds memory_notes.admitted (default 1, so every existing note
stays live). Tests cover: a proposal is out of recall until admitted, a rejected
proposal never reaches recall, and admitting supersedes the prior team decision.

Add a sessions_for_file (blame) tool to the MCP server

`motif blame`, from the code back to the conversation, was CLI-only. An agent
about to change a file could recall a topic but not ask which sessions produced
this exact file. The endpoint (/api/sessions/by-file) and client method already
existed; this surfaces them over MCP so any agent can do "why is this file like
this" natively.

The endpoint and the MCP local backend now share one sessionsTouchingFile
helper that pushes the team-or-owner visibility predicate into SQL, so a large
history is filtered by the database rather than loaded to filter every row in
memory (which also closes the endpoint's unbounded pre-filter scan).

Weaver runs Codex too, not just Claude Code

defaultRunAgent hardcoded `claude`, so on a machine with only Codex every
Weaver job failed with "claude CLI unavailable", contradicting the README's
"your own Claude/Codex". It now tries Claude Code first and, only when that
CLI is absent (ENOENT, not a run failure), falls back to `codex exec` in a
workspace-write sandbox with the prompt on stdin, the same dispatch the ask
path already uses. A run failure from an installed agent still surfaces as-is
rather than silently retrying on the other tool.

Close privacy seams from solo memory; fix Cursor, mention and search edges

Distilling personal sessions made three latent privacy seams reachable,
all now closed:
- an orphaned personal note (source session deleted) coalesces its
  visibility with orphan_visibility before the Weaver-queue check, so it
  can no longer leak into a broadcast draft-PR job;
- /api/overview's decision and conflict counts get the same visibility
  gate as every sibling count in the handler;
- the live memory-updated / memory-conflict / memory-reviewed events now
  carry the source note's owner, and the SSE gate withholds a personal
  session's distilled activity from non-owners.

Unrelated correctness fixes found in the same review:
- a corrupt Cursor timestamp no longer throws out of readCursorSession
  and drops the whole conversation;
- @mention matching respects word boundaries, so @benjamin no longer
  notifies a member named ben;
- searchSessions returns nothing for an empty query instead of throwing
  a raw FTS error over the MCP search tool.

Memory works solo: distil personal sessions into an owner-private lane

The distiller only processed team sessions, so a solo user, whose
sessions are all personal, got an empty memory and nothing to recall.
Personal sessions are now distilled too, into a private lane their owner
alone can read.

The two lanes stay honest without leaking:
- context: a run sees team notes plus, for a personal run, that member's
  own personal notes, so private memory never bleeds into a shared note's
  extraction prompt.
- supersession is lane-scoped: a personal session can never silently
  retire a team decision, only add or flag alongside it.
- conflict stays cross-lane but never replaces the current note, so a
  personal insight can flag disagreement (owner-only) without the team
  losing anything.
- confidence support is counted only among notes the viewer can see, so
  one member's private session never lifts another's confidence.

A note's lane is derived from its source session, so it always matches
what recall, the review queue and the graph read back. Recall labels a
personal note "your memory" rather than "team memory".
